name: Toya Analysis Ontology v3
purpose: Turn recurring analytical reasoning from POCs into executable priors, guardrails, evidence gates, and escalation rules for Survey CSV Analyzer.
north_star: Generate a hypothesis, verify it against raw evidence, search for exceptions, reconstruct the DGP, and only then model.
core_principles: Analyzer-generated schema summaries are hypotheses, not truth; verify raw shape, column names, boundary rows, and value patterns before accepting a structural diagnosis.
Every high-severity structural diagnosis should carry an evidence status: confirmed, rejected, or unresolved.
High missingness is not automatically poor data quality; test whether it is conditional on eligibility, routing, wave, or an option-to-free-text relationship.
When an ID-like field is unique and no repeated structure is detected, explicitly record respondent-level rows as a provisional analytical-unit hypothesis rather than keeping a permanent warning.
Do not treat schema labels as truth; validate variable meaning with values, ranges, missingness, and neighboring structure.
Rows are not automatically independent analytical units; infer repeated, nested, clustered, or expanded observations before modeling.
A visible pattern is only a starting hypothesis; actively search for exceptions and contradictions.
Reconstruct the likely data-generating process before interpreting associations.
Can analyze is not the same as should analyze; stop or simplify when information is insufficient for a stable model.
Missingness can encode study design, workflow, or eligibility rather than random data loss.
Constructed scales should be validated before being used as outcomes or predictors.
Separate statistical significance from substantive importance, predictive value, and decision usefulness.
Match validation strategy to the intended generalization target: new person, new time/wave, new group/country, or new setting.
When current data cannot answer the real question, identify the missing variable, external dataset, or domain mechanism needed next.

guardrails.trigger: column labels/types conflict with observed values or workbook structure
guardrails.action: block inferential modeling until schema/value-range issues are surfaced
examples: Google serial dates treated as ordinary numeric values

guardrails.trigger: any schema-collapse, header-mixing, row-unit, or structural-missingness hypothesis is raised
guardrails.action: verify the hypothesis against raw dataframe evidence and label it confirmed, rejected, or unresolved before allowing it to drive preprocessing/model choice
examples: Unnamed-column hypothesis rejected when raw columns are named
rows-not-units warning rejected when respondent ID is unique and no repeated structure is detected

guardrails.trigger: repeated IDs, stage/wave/day/panel structure, expanded rows, or clustering candidates
guardrails.action: report row N and likely independent-unit N separately; prefer cluster-aware/repeated-measure reasoning
report uniqueness and duplicate counts; if unique with no competing repeat structure, mark one-row-per-unit as provisionally supported

guardrails.trigger: binary outcome has fewer than 20 events or events-per-planned-predictor is low
guardrails.action: warn against ordinary high-dimensional logistic regression; prefer descriptive, parsimonious, penalized, Bayesian, or exact/Firth-style alternatives

guardrails.trigger: multiple similarly named Likert/binary items or precomputed composite scale
guardrails.action: inspect item distributions and reliability/structure before outcome modeling

guardrails.trigger: many outcomes x many predictors or repeated item-level hypothesis tests
guardrails.action: flag multiplicity; prioritize hypotheses or apply FDR/other correction when appropriate

guardrails.trigger: aggregate variable and its component variables appear together
guardrails.action: flag redundancy/multicollinearity and explain interpretation shift if modeled jointly

guardrails.trigger: missingness differs sharply by wave/period/group/time or follows protocol boundaries
guardrails.action: treat missingness as potentially design-generated; do not default to MCAR language

guardrails.trigger: many columns share the same missing rows or row-level missingness forms a small number of repeated signatures
guardrails.action: treat this as a survey-routing/eligibility hypothesis; report the signature counts and candidate effective analysis N rather than deleting high-missing columns mechanically

guardrails.trigger: free-text/FA column has a similarly named base option or dummy column
guardrails.action: check whether free-text nonmissingness is conditionally aligned with the base option; if aligned, classify missingness as expected routing rather than data loss

guardrails.trigger: observational, voluntary exposure, nonrandom treatment, or protocol-confounded comparison
guardrails.action: use association language unless identification assumptions are justified

guardrails.trigger: very large sample where trivial effects can be highly significant
guardrails.action: foreground effect size, uncertainty, incremental value, and out-of-sample performance rather than p-values alone

questions: Is there a stated-revealed gap?
Do predictors act differently on stated preference and actual behavior?
Are expected positive relationships contradicted by observed behavior?
cautions: Do not equate stated WTP with market demand.
A gap may reflect hypothetical bias, context, liquidity, prices, design, or measurement differences.

questions: Was exposure randomized, voluntary, or introduced only in part of the study?
Who selects into exposure?
Does effect heterogeneity exist?
cautions: Selection adjustment does not remove unobserved confounding.
Protocol timing can be confounded with treatment.

questions: What is the true analytical unit?
Are observations nested or repeated?
What level should uncertainty/generalization target?
cautions: Random row split may leak group/time information.

questions: Are item responses internally coherent?
Is a composite justified?
Should scale-level results be decomposed to item-level interpretation?
cautions: Do not mechanically average items with weak or contradictory structure.
Small N can make complex factor models unstable.

questions: Is there an expected order?
Which observations violate the dominant sequence?
Are intervals skewed or implausible?
cautions: A detected dominant order is a hypothesis, not automatically the domain definition.

questions: What simple rule predicts observed choices?
Which high-scoring cases were not chosen?
What unrecorded constraint could explain those exceptions?
cautions: Do not invent the hidden business rule; present candidate mechanisms as hypotheses/questions.

questions: Is missingness concentrated in specific periods/groups?
Was a variable introduced later or only asked conditionally?
cautions: Do not call structured missingness random without evidence.

questions: Was this variable directly observed, externally assigned, or derived?
Could external data unlock the real mechanism?
Does a domain-derived variable better match the question?
cautions: Proxy variables must not be described as direct measurements.
Derived values inherit assumptions from their construction.

questions: Is statistical significance practically meaningful?
What is the intended target of generalization?
Should validation hold out time/groups instead of random rows?
cautions: High AUC from group identifiers may not imply transportability to unseen groups.

questions: Do blocks of questions disappear for the same respondents?
Does a free-text field appear only when its paired option is selected?
What is the effective N after eligibility/routing?
cautions: Do not interpret expected skip-pattern blanks as ordinary missing data.
Do not infer code meanings without questionnaire/codebook evidence.

cross_cutting_reasoning.name: Hypothesis -> Raw Evidence -> Verdict
procedure: State the structural hypothesis explicitly.
Inspect raw shape, columns, boundary rows, IDs, missingness signatures, and paired fields that bear on it.
Assign confirmed, rejected, or unresolved.
Only confirmed findings may automatically change preprocessing; unresolved findings remain cautions.

cross_cutting_reasoning.name: Expected Pattern -> Exception
procedure: Find the dominant pattern.
Identify observations that should follow it but do not.
Quantify the exceptions.
Search for variables or protocol rules that explain them.
Ask the user when the mechanism is not observed.

cross_cutting_reasoning.name: Observed Data -> Data Generating Process
procedure: Identify collection units and timing.
Infer treatment/eligibility/protocol boundaries.
Separate raw, derived, and externally assigned variables.
Check whether missingness and coding reflect the process.
Only then select models.

cross_cutting_reasoning.name: Dataset Boundary Check
procedure: Ask what can be answered from the current table.
Identify unanswered mechanisms.
Look for date/location/domain keys that could join external data.
Propose the smallest additional data needed.

cross_cutting_reasoning.name: Model Evolution
procedure: Start with descriptive benchmark.
Fit/consider the simplest model that answers the question.
Diagnose violations/instability.
Escalate only when the next model addresses a specific limitation.
Validate at the level of intended generalization.

analysis_escalation: 0. Raw evidence gate: verify actual shape, raw column names, boundary rows, obvious header/footer contamination, and any prior schema diagnosis.
0.5. Survey-routing audit: inspect repeated missingness signatures, eligibility/screening candidates, paired option/free-text fields, and candidate effective N.
1. Variable audit: type, range, special codes, provenance, missingness, composite/derived variables.
2. Unit/design audit: true independent unit, repetition/nesting, treatment timing, protocol boundaries, rare events.
3. Descriptive benchmark: distributions, group summaries, trajectories, stated-revealed gaps.
4. Pattern-exception pass: actively identify contradictions, outliers, and high-value exceptions.
5. Core contrast aligned with the decision/research question.
6. Scale validation / balance / missingness mechanism checks when triggered.
7. Parsimonious adjusted model only when information supports it.
8. Heterogeneity/interactions only when theory/design and sample size justify them.
9. Robustness and validation matched to the generalization target.
interpretation_rules: For survey routing, report raw N and candidate effective N separately, and distinguish expected skip-pattern blanks from unexplained missingness.
Do not repeat an Analyzer-generated structural warning as fact unless raw evidence confirms it; label rejected and unresolved hypotheses explicitly.
Say evidence was insufficient to confirm an association/difference rather than there is no effect when uncertainty is large.
Do not infer causality from observational association or voluntary exposure.
Report row count and effective analytical-unit count separately when repeated/clustered data are plausible.
When binary events are rare, explicitly state event counts before model interpretation.
For large N, emphasize effect size and incremental value rather than p-values alone.
For scales, distinguish scale-level findings from item-level findings and report reliability limitations.
Treat exceptions as analytically informative rather than noise by default.
Describe missingness as structural/design-related when evidence supports it.
Distinguish direct measurements from proxies, external assignments, and derived variables.
Always end with what the result changes for the decision/research question and what evidence would change the conclusion.
